abstract: |
  This study asks whether a researcher-level fixed effect estimated from bibliometric panel data reflects individual ability or a persistent, environment-driven component of the researcher's surroundings. Using the publication histories of 9,843 researchers in the top six economics journals (1970--2016), I estimate a time-invariant human-capital proxy from a cohort-percentile citation panel and design a test that separates a researcher's actual coauthors, whose quality is endogenous to the researcher's own ability, from researchers who were merely co-located at the same institution in the same years but never coauthored. The same panel is also used to test a natural secondary question motivating its construction---whether the early-1990s diffusion of information and communication technology (ICT) reshaped the ability premium in economics publishing. A researcher-level fixed effect estimated from panel data on citations, output, or pay is routinely interpreted as a portable, time-invariant measure of individual ability. But such an effect is estimated jointly with a time-varying environment---coauthors, institutions, funding, and networks---that the individual does not fully choose and that may itself shape realized performance. Whether the estimated effect reflects ability net of this environment, or is contaminated by a persistent environmental component, is rarely tested directly, because a researcher's environment is typically chosen in a way that is correlated with their own unobserved ability, confounding any simple comparison.

This study develops a test that separates these two possibilities using the publication histories of the top six economics journals---*American Economic Review*, *Econometrica*, *Journal of Political Economy*, *Quarterly Journal of Economics*, *Review of Economic Studies*, and *Review of Economics and Statistics* (hereafter T6). After estimating a time-invariant human-capital proxy for each of 9,843 researchers (1970--2016), I compare researchers' actual early-career coauthors, whose quality is endogenous to the researcher's own ability, to researchers who were merely co-located at the same institution in the same years but never coauthored---a source of exposure to peer quality that is far less correlated with a researcher's own ability. A researcher's own long-run performance is then regressed on this peer-quality measure with and without an institution fixed effect, isolating a within-institution effect of peer quality from a between-institution confound common to all researchers at historically strong institutions.

The same T6 publication panel also provides a natural setting to examine a second, more conventional question: whether the early-1990s diffusion of information and communication technology (ICT) reshaped who succeeds in top-journal publishing. The effect of ICT on the distribution of citation outcomes can be decomposed into two channels. The returns channel posits that ICT operates complementarily with high-ability researchers, amplifying the ability premium, consistent with the skill-biased technological change (SBTC) hypothesis in labor economics. The threshold channel posits that ICT instead lowers the cost of access to data, software, and communication infrastructure, allowing researchers who previously could not surpass the T6 entry threshold to enter, without necessarily changing the return to ability itself.

This study contributes to three strands of the literature. First, it adapts the logic of [@azoulay_zivin_wang2010]'s exogenous-shock peer-effects design to a co-location rather than a coauthorship comparison, providing direct evidence that early-career exposure to strong peers operates through resource congestion rather than a positive ability spillover, once institutional prestige is netted out. Second, it applies the interactive fixed-effects factor model of [@Bai2009] to economics T6 publication histories to estimate the time-invariant human-capital proxy used throughout, and formally tests whether the added flexibility of the interactive specification is warranted relative to a simpler additive alternative. Third, it reinterprets the 1990s transition in economics research documented by [@Hamermesh2013] and [@angrist_etal2020] from the perspective of micro-level researcher cohorts entering T6 before versus after 1992.

# Literature Review {#sec-literature}

This study relates to four strands of the literature. The first pertains to the peer-effects and exogenous-shock literature on how a researcher's environment shapes measured performance. The second concerns methodological research on measuring researcher-specific time-invariant ability from panel citation data. The third involves micro-empirical studies on the production function of economics research output. The fourth examines citation patterns in economics and the 1990s turning point.

[@azoulay_zivin_wang2010] use the sudden deaths of eminent scientists as an exogenous shock to their collaborators' research environment and find that surviving coauthors' subsequent output declines, a pattern the authors attribute to the loss of access to the deceased superstar's resources and networks rather than to a loss of inspiration alone. This literature motivates the central methodological concern of this study: any procedure that infers ability from an individual fixed effect estimated jointly with a time-varying collaboration environment risks capturing the quality of researchers around an individual rather than a purely time-invariant personal trait. Section V develops a design that exploits co-location without actual coauthorship to isolate this concern from genuine assortative matching on ability, extending [@azoulay_zivin_wang2010]'s exit-based shock to an entry-based comparison.

[@Bai2009] proposes a panel data model in which the outcome of unit $i$ at time $t$ is decomposed into a unit-specific loading $\lambda_i$ interacted with a common time factor $F_t$, in addition to conventional additive fixed effects. Unlike an additive two-way fixed-effects model, the interactive specification $Y_{it}=\lambda_i F_t+\varepsilon_{it}$ allows the shape of the common time profile, not merely its level, to be scaled differently across units, and is estimated by iterative principal components on the (possibly incomplete) outcome matrix. This provides the theoretical basis for the human-capital proxy---the loading $\hat\lambda_i$, or, where the added flexibility is not empirically warranted, the additive author fixed effect $\hat\alpha_i$---whose origins the peer-environment design above interrogates. Section III develops both specifications and selects between them on out-of-sample predictive grounds.

[@angrist_diederichs2024] estimate the production function of citation outcomes at the economics doctoral dissertation level and show that observable inputs explain only a fraction of the performance variance. The present study absorbs part of this residual variation through author fixed effects $\hat\alpha_i$ and interprets them as an indicator of unobservable human capital, while directly testing, in Section VI, how much of that residual reflects a persistent institutional environment rather than the individual alone.

Changes in publication and citation patterns within economics have been analyzed in several studies. [@Hamermesh2013] analyzes 60 years of publication patterns in the top three economics journals and shows that the point at which empirical research overtook theoretical research was the early 1990s. Since this period coincides with the mass diffusion of ICT, it provides a key justification for this study's use of 1992 as the cohort demarcation point in its secondary analysis of technological diffusion. In a subsequent study, [@hamermesh2018] discusses the usefulness of a 10-year citation window in reducing truncation bias for junior researchers, which provides the rationale for this study's use of 10-year cumulative citations as the primary citation measure. [@angrist_etal2020] show that citations from outside the discipline to economics papers increased substantially after the 1990s, suggesting that post-ICT citation changes are related not only to within-field scale expansion but also to the broadening of interdisciplinary influence.

Compared to the above literature, this study's contributions are as follows. First, it adapts the logic of [@azoulay_zivin_wang2010] to a co-location rather than a coauthorship design, providing direct evidence that early-career exposure to strong peers operates through resource congestion rather than a positive ability spillover, once institutional prestige is netted out. Second, it implements the [@Bai2009] interactive fixed-effects model on economics T6 publication histories and shows, via out-of-sample cross-validation, that a far simpler additive specification performs equivalently, favoring parsimony over the interactive model's additional identification burden. Third, it uses Hamermesh's early-1990s breakpoint to compare the human-capital distribution between incumbent and new T6 cohorts, and tests directly for a discrete calendar-year citation shock coincident with ICT diffusion.

# Theoretical Framework {#sec-theory}

## Ability, Technology, and Resources

A researcher's citation outcome is taken to depend on three conceptually distinct inputs: time-invariant human capital $H_i$ (the researcher's own ability), the period-specific technological environment $T_t$ (data access, computation, and dissemination infrastructure common to all researchers at a point in time), and time-varying research resources $K_{i,t}$, including institutional prestige and coauthor networks. This distinction serves two purposes below. First, because raw citation counts are also driven by secular growth in the size of the citing literature---an artifact of $T_t$ rather than of $H_i$---this study normalizes citation counts before estimation: each paper's 10-year citation count is converted into its percentile rank among all papers published in the same calendar year (Section III.A), so that the estimated author-level parameter reflects standing relative to same-vintage peers rather than the vintage itself. Second, the distinction between $H_i$ and $K_{i,t}$ is used directly in Section VI.F to ask whether the estimated author effect reflects ability alone or a persistent, resource-driven component of a researcher's environment.

## Two Operating Channels of the ICT Shock

Within this framework, ICT can affect citation outcomes through two channels. The first is the returns channel. If ICT combines complementarily with high-ability researchers, then citation outcomes of high-ability researchers should increase disproportionately after ICT diffusion, consistent with the SBTC hypothesis. Empirically, this channel would manifest as (i) a discrete, economy-wide upward shift in citation levels timed to ICT diffusion and (ii) a widening of the human-capital distribution driven by gains concentrated among already high-$H_i$ researchers.

The second is the threshold channel. If ICT lowers the cost of access to data, software, and communication infrastructure, the resource constraints required for T6 entry are relaxed, allowing researchers who could not previously surpass the entry threshold to enter. This channel predicts an expansion of the *entering* cohort's ability distribution, including its lower tail, without necessarily requiring any change in the return to ability itself.

Section VI evaluates both channels directly. No discrete, economy-wide citation-level shock coincident with ICT diffusion is found (Section VI.E), which weighs against the returns channel operating through the citation technology itself. The post-1992 T6-entry cohort's human-capital distribution is significantly wider than the pre-1992 cohort's (Section VI.C), consistent in principle with either channel, but this widening is concentrated among researchers who collaborate in large teams rather than uniformly across the distribution (Section VI.D), and a direct test of whether large-team collaboration became a *more* rewarded technology after 1992 finds no significant change in that return (Section VI.D). Taken together, the evidence is more consistent with the threshold channel reshaping who enters T6 than with a straightforward amplification of the ability premium. These tests, however, target an aggregate level shock and the return to a single collaboration technology; they do not directly assess whether the correlation between an incumbent's already-established ability and subsequent performance strengthened after ICT diffusion, a more general test of the returns channel that would require an individual-level before/after comparison not pursued here. Section VI.F additionally documents a third, previously unmodeled channel operating through $K_{i,t}$: early-career exposure to an unusually strong local peer cohort is associated with *worse*, not better, long-run relative performance once between-institution differences are removed, consistent with congestion for scarce mentorship and collaboration resources rather than a positive spillover into $H_i$.

# Statistical Methods {#sec-methods}

## Cohort-Percentile Normalization {#sec-pctile}

For each paper $p$ published in calendar year $y(p)$, let $c_p$ denote its 10-year cumulative citation count. The cohort percentile is

$$
\text{pctile}_p \;=\; \frac{\operatorname{rank}(c_p \mid y(p))}{N_{y(p)}},
$$ {#eq-pctile}

where the rank is taken among all sample papers published in the same calendar year $y(p)$ and $N_{y(p)}$ is the size of that publication-year cohort. Author--academic-age cells are then formed by averaging $\text{pctile}_p$ over all papers a given author published at a given academic age $a_{i,t}=t-\text{first}_i$. This construction places every calendar era on the same 0--1 scale of relative standing and, by design, cannot detect a shock that shifts an entire publication-year cohort's citation level uniformly; Section V.B therefore supplements it with a level-based specification for that purpose.

## The Interactive Fixed-Effects Model {#sec-ife}

Let $Y_{it}$ denote the cohort-percentile outcome of author $i$ at academic age $t\in\{0,\dots,30\}$. Following [@Bai2009], the baseline specification is

$$
Y_{it} \;=\; \lambda_i F_t + \varepsilon_{it},
$$ {#eq-ife}

where $\lambda_i$ is a researcher-specific loading interpreted as time-invariant human capital and $F_t$ is a common academic-age profile shared by all researchers. Because the author--age panel is sparse (only academic ages at which an author actually published are observed), (@eq-ife) is estimated by a hard-impute algorithm: missing cells are initialized at the sample mean, a rank-one singular value decomposition of the resulting complete matrix is computed, missing cells are replaced by the low-rank reconstruction while observed cells are reset to their true values, and the procedure iterates to convergence. By the Eckart--Young theorem, each iteration solves the least-squares rank-one approximation problem exactly conditional on the current fill-in, so the procedure is a matrix-completion analogue of [@Bai2009]'s iterative principal-components estimator. Because the product $\lambda_i F_t$ is invariant to rescaling $(\lambda_i,F_t)\mapsto(c\lambda_i,F_t/c)$, the sign of $F_t$ is fixed so that its mean is positive, and $\hat\lambda_i$ is reported as a percentile rank across authors rather than in its native (arbitrary) scale.

## Model Selection: An Additive Alternative {#sec-modelselect}

The interactive specification (@eq-ife) is strictly more flexible than, and nests as a special case, the additive two-way fixed-effects model

$$
Y_{it} \;=\; \alpha_i + \gamma_t + \varepsilon_{it},
$$ {#eq-additive}

in which every researcher is assumed to share an identical academic-age profile $\gamma_t$ up to a level shift $\alpha_i$, rather than a profile that can also be rescaled in shape by $\lambda_i$. Because the additional flexibility of (@eq-ife) carries an identification cost---the sign and rotation indeterminacy of factor models, and a higher effective parameter count per author when extended beyond rank one---this study selects between the two specifications on the basis of five-fold out-of-sample cross-validation over observed author--age cells, rather than by in-sample fit alone. Held-out cells are masked as unobserved during re-estimation, and predictive $R^2$ is computed against a held-out-mean benchmark. This comparison, together with a null-data placebo check, is reported in Section VI.B; the additive specification (@eq-additive) is preferred throughout the remainder of the paper on the strength of that comparison, and $\hat\alpha_i$ is used as the primary human-capital proxy.

# Data {#sec-data}

## Data Sources

The publication data for this study were collected in three stages through the Elsevier Scopus API. First, metadata for article and review categories from the six T6 journals published since 1970 were collected, identifying 13,287 unique authors. Second, the complete publication histories of these authors, including non-T6 publications, were tracked to construct a panel of 431,874 author--paper rows corresponding to 335,558 unique papers. Third, the Scopus CitationOverview API was used to compute 10-year cumulative citations for each paper after publication.

## Construction of the Analytic Sample

Author--academic-age cells were formed for academic ages 0 through 30 using the cohort-percentile outcome of Section III.A, averaging multiple papers published by the same author at the same academic age into a single cell. Authors observed at fewer than two distinct academic ages---for whom author and academic-age effects cannot be jointly identified---were dropped. This restriction reduces the 13,287 T6 authors to a final analytic sample of 9,843 authors, observed in 112,091 of $9{,}843\times31=305{,}133$ possible author--age cells (36.7% density).

## Cohort Definitions {#sec-cohort-def}

Following [@Hamermesh2013]'s early-1990s breakpoint, each author is assigned to one of two cohorts based on the calendar year of their *first T6-journal* publication (which need not coincide with their first publication in any journal, used to define academic age above).

| Group | T6 Entry Criterion | $N$ | Interpretation |
|------------------|:-----------------------------------|---:|------------------|
| $C^1$ | First T6 publication before 1992 | 1,919 | incumbent |
| $C^2$ | First T6 publication in or after 1992 | 7,924 | new T6 entrant |

: Cohort definitions {#tbl-cohort-def}

If ICT operated through the threshold channel, the $\hat\alpha_i$ distribution of $C^2$ should be wider, and possibly shifted, relative to $C^1$. Section VI.C examines this implication directly.

## Unit of Analysis and Dependent Variable

The unit of analysis is the combination of author $i$ and academic age $t$ (Sections III.A--III.B), except in Section VI.E, which instead indexes observations by calendar year to test directly for an economy-wide citation-level shock; that specification uses $\ln(1+c_{i,t})$, the untransformed log citation count, rather than the cohort percentile, since the percentile transform is by construction invariant to a shock that shifts an entire cohort uniformly.

# Empirical Strategy {#sec-strategy}

## Cohort Comparison Across the 1992 T6-Entry Threshold {#sec-strategy-cohort}

(@eq-additive) is estimated separately within $C^1$ and $C^2$ (Section IV.C), yielding cohort-specific academic-age profiles $\hat\gamma_t^{C^1}, \hat\gamma_t^{C^2}$ and human-capital distributions $\{\hat\alpha_i\}_{i\in C^1}$, $\{\hat\alpha_i\}_{i\in C^2}$. The two distributions are compared by a two-sample Kolmogorov--Smirnov test and a Welch $t$-test. To probe mechanism, the comparison is further stratified by two author-level collaboration measures computed over each author's full publication history: the share of an author's papers with coauthors affiliated with more than one country, and the author's mean number of coauthors per paper. If the threshold channel operates specifically through lowering the cost of large-team or internationally distributed collaboration, the widening of the $C^2$ distribution should be concentrated in the corresponding subgroup.

## Testing for a Direct Calendar-Year ICT Effect {#sec-strategy-breaks}

Because the cohort-percentile outcome cannot detect a shock common to an entire publication-year cohort, this study additionally estimates a level-based specification with an explicit calendar-year fixed effect,

$$
\ln(1+c_{i,t}) \;=\; \gamma_{y(i,t)} + \lambda_i F_t + \varepsilon_{it}, \qquad y(i,t)=\text{first}_i+t,
$$ {#eq-yearfe}

jointly with the rank-one interactive age factor, by alternating between an OLS regression on year dummies and the hard-impute update of Section III.B. The resulting calendar-year effects $\hat\gamma_y$ are then tested for an unknown structural break using a Quandt--Andrews-style scan: for each candidate break year $\tau$, a piecewise-linear regression of $\hat\gamma_y$ on year, weighted by the number of underlying observations, is estimated with a slope shift at $\tau$, and an $F$-test of no slope change is computed. The candidate year with the largest $F$-statistic is the data-implied break point; a comparably large $F$-statistic specifically at a year in the 1993--2000 ICT-diffusion window would constitute direct evidence for the returns channel.

## Peer-Environment Design: Separating Ability from Resource Congestion {#sec-strategy-peer}

To test whether $\hat\alpha_i$ reflects time-invariant ability $H_i$ or a persistent, resource-driven component of $K_{i,t}$, two peer-quality measures are constructed from each author's first four academic-age years ($a_{i,t}\in\{0,1,2,3\}$). The first, $\overline{\alpha}_i^{\text{coauth}}$, is the mean $\hat\alpha$ of an author's actual early-career coauthors. Because coauthor choice is endogenous to ability, a second, more plausibly exogenous measure, $\overline{\alpha}_i^{\text{peer}}$, is constructed from researchers who published from the *same institution in the same or an adjacent calendar year* as the focal author but who never coauthored with that author at any point in either researcher's career. Both measures are regressed on the author's own long-run (academic ages 15--25) cohort-percentile performance, controlling for the author's own early-career (academic ages 0--3) performance, with and without a fixed effect for the author's modal early-career institution. Following the logic of [@azoulay_zivin_wang2010], comparing the pooled and within-institution estimates isolates a genuine peer-to-peer effect from a confound common to all researchers at historically strong institutions.

# Estimation Results {#sec-results}

## Basic Properties of the $\hat\alpha_i$ Distribution

Estimating (@eq-additive) on the full analytic sample recovers $\hat\alpha_i$ for all 9,843 authors. The distribution has a mean of $-0.006$, a median of $-0.007$, and a standard deviation of $0.154$, with mild positive skewness (0.21) and near-zero excess kurtosis ($-0.02$); a Shapiro--Wilk test on a random subsample of 5,000 authors gives $W=0.994$. Summary statistics are reported in @tbl-alpha-dist.

| Statistic               |   Value |
|-------------------------|--------:|
| $N$                     |   9,843 |
| Mean                    | $-0.006$ |
| Median                  | $-0.007$ |
| Standard deviation      |    0.154 |
| Minimum                 | $-0.367$ |
| Maximum                 | $+0.583$ |
| Skewness                |   $+0.21$ |
| Excess kurtosis         |   $-0.02$ |
| Shapiro--Wilk statistic ($n=5{,}000$) | $0.994$ |

: $\hat\alpha_i$ distribution summary: 9,843 authors {#tbl-alpha-dist}

## Model Selection: Interactive versus Additive Specifications {#sec-results-modelselect}

@tbl-modelselect compares the in-sample and five-fold out-of-sample $R^2$ of the interactive model (@eq-ife) and the additive model (@eq-additive), together with two uninformative benchmarks (an author-mean-only and an academic-age-mean-only predictor) and a placebo check in which the observed cohort-percentile values are randomly permuted across author--age cells before re-estimation, holding the missingness pattern fixed.

| Model | In-sample $R^2$ | Out-of-sample $R^2$ |
|---|---:|---:|
| Author-mean only | -- | 0.102 |
| Academic-age-mean only | -- | 0.031 |
| Additive, $\alpha_i+\gamma_t$ | 0.308 | **0.132** |
| Interactive, $\lambda_iF_t$ ($r=1$) | 0.308 | 0.132 |
| Placebo (randomly permuted values) | 0.087 | $-0.132$ |

: Model comparison via five-fold out-of-sample cross-validation {#tbl-modelselect}

Three results are notable. First, the interactive and additive specifications are statistically indistinguishable both in-sample (0.308 versus 0.308) and out-of-sample (0.132 versus 0.132), so the added rotation and scale indeterminacy of the interactive model buys no measurable predictive power in this application; the additive $\hat\alpha_i$ is used as the primary human-capital proxy for the remainder of the paper. Second, both specifications substantially outperform either uninformative benchmark, confirming that both author identity and academic age carry genuine, complementary information. Third, the placebo comparison shows that a positive in-sample $R^2$ (0.087) can arise from pure overfitting of the many per-author free parameters even when the underlying data contain no signal, but that this apparent fit collapses to a negative out-of-sample $R^2$ ($-0.132$); because the real-data out-of-sample $R^2$ remains reliably positive (0.132), the fitted model is judged to capture genuine, generalizable structure rather than an artifact of its flexibility.

## Cohort Comparison: Pre- versus Post-1992 T6 Entrants {#sec-results-cohort}

@tbl-cohort-summary reports the $\hat\alpha_i$ distribution separately for the incumbent ($C^1$) and new-entrant ($C^2$) cohorts defined in @tbl-cohort-def.

| Statistic | $C^1$ incumbent (pre-1992) | $C^2$ new T6 (post-1992) |
|---|---:|---:|
| $N$ | 1,919 | 7,924 |
| Mean $\hat\alpha_i$ | $-0.019$ | $-0.001$ |
| SD $\hat\alpha_i$ | 0.135 | **0.160** |

: $\hat\alpha_i$ distribution by T6-entry cohort {#tbl-cohort-summary}

A two-sample Kolmogorov--Smirnov test rejects equality of the two distributions ($D=0.067$, $p=1.6\times10^{-6}$), and the standard deviation of $\hat\alpha_i$ is 18.3% larger in the post-1992 cohort. This pattern also holds for the interactive-model loading $\hat\lambda_i$ (pre-1992 SD $=0.713$; post-1992 SD $=0.911$; $D=0.075$, $p=6.2\times10^{-8}$), so the finding is not an artifact of the choice between Equations (@eq-ife) and (@eq-additive). Because $C^1$ and $C^2$ are defined by *entry cohort* rather than by a fixed calendar date, and because a researcher's academic age at any given calendar year is mechanically determined by entry cohort, this comparison cannot on its own separate a genuine period effect of ICT diffusion from an ordinary age-cohort pattern in which more recently entering researchers are, on average, earlier in their careers and hence more heterogeneous. Sections VI.D and VI.E probe this distinction further.

## Heterogeneity by Collaboration Structure {#sec-results-hetero}

@tbl-subgroup stratifies the cohort comparison of Section VI.C by whether an author's collaboration intensity (mean coauthors per paper) and international-collaboration share are above or below the sample median.

| Subgroup | Pre-1992 SD | Post-1992 SD | \% increase |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| High international collaboration | 0.136 | 0.158 | 16.7% |
| Low international collaboration | 0.135 | 0.163 | 20.4% |
| Small collaboration team | 0.135 | 0.154 | 14.3% |
| **Large collaboration team** | 0.133 | **0.162** | **21.5%** |

: Growth in $\hat\alpha_i$ dispersion by collaboration subgroup {#tbl-subgroup}

The widening of the human-capital distribution is essentially uniform across international-collaboration subgroups (16.7% versus 20.4%) but is markedly larger among authors who typically publish in larger teams (21.5% versus 14.3%). If ICT lowered the cost of forming and coordinating large research teams, this pattern is consistent with the threshold channel operating specifically through team-based collaboration technology. However, a direct interaction regression of $\hat\alpha_i$ on mean team size, an indicator for post-1993 T6 entry, and their interaction finds no significant change in the *return* to team size across cohorts (interaction coefficient $-0.004$, $p=0.23$): teams grew larger after the early 1990s, but collaborating in a larger team did not become a significantly more rewarded strategy. The subgroup pattern in @tbl-subgroup is therefore better read as corroborating evidence of a cohort-level compositional shift than as evidence against a change in the return to ability more generally, since this interaction speaks only to the team-size channel specifically.

## No Evidence of a Discrete Calendar-Year ICT Effect {#sec-results-breaks}

Estimating (@eq-yearfe) on the full sample (1927--2016, 88 distinct calendar years) yields an overall fit of $R^2=0.410$. The Quandt--Andrews-style scan of Section V.B, restricted to calendar years with at least 50 underlying observations, identifies its largest slope break at **1983** ($F=114.2$), where the annual growth rate of $\hat\gamma_y$ rises from 0.024 to 0.068---a break of a magnitude far beyond what the number of candidate years scanned could plausibly generate by chance. By contrast, every candidate break year in the 1991--2000 ICT-diffusion window shows a markedly smaller $F$-statistic that declines smoothly as the candidate moves away from 1983 (from $F=44.9$ at 1991 to $F=5.2$ at 2000), the signature of a single break's statistical shadow rather than an independent second break. No candidate year in the ICT-diffusion window is distinguishable from this decaying tail.

A break at 1983 predates ICT diffusion by roughly a decade and is not easily given a substantive interpretation; a natural candidate is a change in Scopus's own indexing coverage of older journal issues rather than a genuine shift in researcher behavior. Consistent with a data-coverage explanation, the growth rate of the number of distinct journals indexed in the underlying corpus, and of the number of observed author--age cells, both show an independent structural break in the same direction five years earlier, at 1977--1978 ($F=564$--$568$), though the offset in timing and the fact that these series *decelerate* rather than accelerate after their own break means the two patterns are not mechanically identical. One auxiliary series does align with the ICT-diffusion window: the mean number of coauthors per paper shows an accelerating growth break at 1993--1997 ($F\approx73$), the only structural break located in this study that coincides with the diffusion period. Taken together, these results provide no evidence of a discrete, economy-wide citation-level shock attributable to ICT, but do corroborate the compositional shift toward larger research teams documented in Section VI.D.

## Peer Environment and the Origins of $\hat\alpha_i$ {#sec-results-peer}

@tbl-peer-effects reports the peer-environment design of Section V.C in three progressively more demanding specifications of

$$
\text{pctile}_i^{\text{late}} = \beta_0 + \beta_1\,\text{pctile}_i^{\text{early}} + \beta_2\,\overline{\alpha}_i^{\text{peer or coauth}} + \eta_{j(i)} + u_i,
$$ {#eq-peer-spec}

where $\eta_{j(i)}$ is a fixed effect for the author's modal early-career institution.

| Spec. | Peer measure | Own early coef. | Peer coef. | $N$ | Institutions | $R^2$ |
|---|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| (1) Coauthors | $\overline{\alpha}_i^{\text{coauth}}$ | 0.062\* | 0.245\*\*\* | 2,733 | -- | 0.032 |
| (2) Co-located | $\overline{\alpha}_i^{\text{peer}}$ | 0.121\*\*\* | 0.173\*\*\* | 3,923 | -- | 0.021 |
| (3) Institution FE | $\overline{\alpha}_i^{\text{peer}}$ | 0.116\*\*\* | $-0.358$\*\*\* | 3,923 | 420 | 0.024 (within) |

: Progressive robustness of the early-career peer-quality coefficient in (@eq-peer-spec) {#tbl-peer-effects}

*Note*: \*$p<0.05$, \*\*$p<0.01$, \*\*\*$p<0.001$. Specification (1) restricts the peer measure to an author's actual coauthors on papers published at academic age 0--3 and controls for own early-career percentile alone (unconditional own-effect coefficient, not tabulated, is 0.104). Specifications (2)--(3) replace this with the mean ability of co-located but never-coauthored researchers observed at the same institution-year cells. Specification (3) additionally absorbs institution fixed effects, so identification rests solely on within-institution variation in peer quality across cohorts entering the same institution at different times.

Two patterns emerge. First, moving from actual coauthors to co-located non-coauthors leaves the coefficient on own early-career performance essentially unchanged (0.121 versus 0.116 across specifications (2)--(3)), whereas including actual coauthor quality roughly halves it (from an unconditional 0.104 to 0.062 in specification (1)); this is consistent with actual-coauthor quality partly proxying for the focal author's own unobserved early-career ability, whereas co-located peer quality---which correlates with own early performance at only $r=0.060$, against $r=0.316$ for actual coauthors---constitutes a comparatively independent and more plausibly exogenous source of variation.

Second, and more strikingly, the sign of the peer-quality coefficient reverses once institution fixed effects are introduced, from $+0.173$ ($p<0.001$) to $-0.358$ ($p<0.001$). The pooled, between-institution estimate is consistent with a simple confound: institutions with historically strong faculty or resources produce both stronger co-located peer pools and stronger long-run outcomes for reasons unrelated to any peer-to-peer transfer of ability. Once this between-institution channel is removed, the within-institution estimate indicates that researchers who happen to enter a given institution during a cohort with an unusually strong contemporaneous peer pool exhibit *worse* long-run relative performance, holding their own early-career percentile fixed. This pattern is consistent with a congestion, or "big fish in a small pond," mechanism, in which a stronger local cohort intensifies competition for scarce mentorship, coauthorship, and visibility resources within $K_{i,t}$, rather than generating a positive knowledge spillover into $H_i$---directly paralleling the resource-loss interpretation of [@azoulay_zivin_wang2010], but operating through crowding at entry rather than through the exit of a senior collaborator.

This result qualifies the structural interpretation of $\hat\alpha_i$ used throughout the paper: part of its cross-sectional variation reflects a persistent, environment-driven component of $K_{i,t}$, operating in a congestion rather than a complementary direction, rather than solely time-invariant ability $H_i$. It also implies that any resource-based threshold channel of ICT (@sec-theory) is unlikely to operate through simple exposure to strong local peers, since such exposure is, if anything, associated with worse rather than better long-run relative outcomes once institutional prestige is netted out.

# Robustness Checks {#sec-robustness}

## Out-of-Sample and Placebo Validation

Section VI.B already reports the central robustness result for the paper's human-capital estimator: a positive five-fold out-of-sample $R^2$ (0.132) that survives cross-validation, contrasted with a placebo specification, constructed by randomly permuting observed outcomes across author--age cells while holding the missingness pattern fixed, whose in-sample fit (0.087) collapses to a negative out-of-sample $R^2$ ($-0.132$). Because the same author-level flexibility that allows the placebo model to overfit noise is also present in the real-data specification, this comparison indicates that the real-data in-sample $R^2$ of 0.308 is itself an overstatement of genuine predictive content, and that the more defensible estimate of the model's explanatory power is the out-of-sample figure of 0.132.

## Construct Validity: Nobel Laureate Verification

To assess whether the estimated $\hat\alpha_i$ is a reasonable proxy for human capital, Nobel laureates in economics were matched to the sample by author identity. Of the 68 laureates recovered in the analytic sample, the mean $\hat\alpha_i$ percentile is 67.0 (against an expected value of 50 under random assignment). @tbl-nobel reports the distributional position of matched laureates in more detail.

| Percentile | Nobel matches | Share |
|------------|--------------:|------:|
| Top 1%     |             2 |  2.9% |
| Top 5%     |             8 | 11.8% |
| Top 10%    |             8 | 11.8% |
| Top 25%    |            30 | 44.1% |
| Top 50%    |            50 | 73.5% |

: Distributional position of Nobel laureates within the $\hat\alpha_i$ distribution {#tbl-nobel}

These results show that $\hat\alpha_i$ is associated with long-term assessments of academic excellence well above chance, though the fact that only 2.9% of matched laureates fall within the top 1% suggests that $\hat\alpha_i$, estimated from a 1970--2016 T6 sample restricted to authors with at least two distinct academic-age observations, is at best a noisy proxy for the very top of the ability distribution---consistent with the interactive-model rank correlations and the peer-environment caveat of Section VI.F, both of which indicate that a meaningful share of variation in $\hat\alpha_i$ is not attributable to stable individual ability alone.

# Discussion and Conclusion {#sec-discussion}

## Summary of Key Findings

This study estimates a time-invariant human-capital proxy for 9,843 researchers based on T6 economics journal publication histories, using an interactive fixed-effects factor model and a simpler additive alternative that is shown, via out-of-sample cross-validation, to perform equivalently and is therefore adopted as the primary estimator. Three findings bear on the paper's central question of whether this proxy reflects ability or environment. First, and central to the paper, an early-career peer-environment design shows that the apparent benefit of strong local peers is entirely a between-institution artifact: once institution fixed effects remove differences in institutional prestige, exposure to an unusually strong contemporaneous peer cohort predicts *worse*, not better, long-run relative performance, consistent with congestion for scarce mentorship and collaboration resources rather than a positive ability spillover. Second, in the paper's secondary application to technological diffusion, researchers entering T6 after the early-1990s ICT-diffusion threshold display a significantly wider human-capital distribution than earlier entrants, concentrated among researchers who collaborate in larger teams, but a direct test finds no corresponding increase in the *return* to large-team collaboration, and a calendar-year structural-break analysis finds no discrete citation-level shock coincident with ICT diffusion at all---evidence more consistent with a compositional shift in who enters T6 than with the threshold channel as commonly formulated, though these tests target an aggregate level shock and the return to team size specifically rather than a general, redistributive change in the return to ability, which this design does not test directly. Third, the Nobel laureate verification supports the construct validity of the human-capital proxy in aggregate, while its imprecision at the very top of the distribution, together with the peer-environment finding, cautions that it should be interpreted as ability net of a non-trivial, resource-driven environmental component rather than as a pure measure of innate researcher quality.
